Miscellaneous Sayings
17.1 A wise and virtuous gentleman
understands the times of flourishing and decline,
is clear about the beginnings of success and failure,
examines the principles of order and chaos,
scrutinizes human nature,
and knows when to advance and when to retreat.
Therefore, even in poverty, he will not dwell in a state on the verge of destruction;
even in poverty, he will not accept the emolument of a corrupt ruler.
Therefore, Tàigōng was seventy years old before he made himself known,
and Sūn Shū'áo resigned from his position as prime minister three times without regret.
Why?
Because they did not forcibly align themselves with those who were not their kind.
Tàigōng's one alliance with Zhōu resulted in his descendants being enfeoffed for seven hundred years,
Sūn Shū'áo's one alliance with Chǔ resulted in his descendants being ennobled for ten generations.
Dàfū Zhǒng preserved the state of Yuè from extinction and helped Gōujiàn achieve hegemony,
but he was later ordered to commit suicide.
Lǐ Sī accumulated merits in Qín but ultimately suffered the Five Punishments.
Both devoted their loyalty and worried about their rulers,
risking their lives to secure the state.
Their merits were the same.
Some were granted titles and their lineages continued uninterrupted,
while others were ordered to commit suicide and suffered punishments.
What they admired and what they followed were different.
Therefore, Jīzi abandoned his state and feigned madness,
Fàn Lǐ left Yuè and changed his name,
Zhì, in the past, served as a younger brother to a ruler and changed his surname.
All these instances demonstrate keen foresight and subtle perception.
He possessed the benevolence to relinquish wealth and influence in order to avoid the nascent seeds of disaster.
For a tyrannical and chaotic ruler,
who would be able to escape bondage in order to employ his own person,
and share in calamity?
Therefore, wise men do not merely fear death and avoid harm,
but understand that sacrificing oneself is useless and only reveals the ruler's tyranny.
Bǐ Gān died serving Zhòu, yet could not rectify his conduct;
Zǐ Xū died serving Wú, yet could not preserve his state.
These two men,
by forcefully remonstrating and dying,
only served to highlight the ruler's tyranny,
without producing any benefit whatsoever, not even the tip of an autumn hair.
Therefore, wise men conceal their wisdom,
shut off their abilities,
and wait until they find the right person before aligning themselves.
Thus, their words will always be heeded,
their actions will never be doubted,
ruler and minister will be in harmony,
and they will be free from worry throughout their lives.
Now, if one has not found the right time,
and also lacks the right person,
but is driven solely by personal inclination,
lamenting the chaos of the world,
worrying about the peril of the ruler,
using a worthless body,
traversing a path of obstruction and concealment,
To pass before slanderous people,
to create limitless lords,
to commit unfathomable crimes,
to injure one's innate nature,
how could one not be deluded!
Therefore, Lord Wén Xìn, Lǐ Sī,
are what the world calls virtuous.
For the sake of the state's plans,
to speculate on the subtle and shoot at the hidden,
this is what is called flawless strategy,
to win battles and seize territory,
this is what is called having no strong enemies.
Accumulating merit was exceedingly great,
power and profit were exceedingly high,
the virtuous were not employed,
the slanderous were employed in affairs,
to know oneself is not employed,
one's benevolence cannot be put aside.
To control the enemy and accumulate merit,
not missing even an autumn hair,
to avoid calamity and remove harm,
not seeing even hills,
to accumulate what one desires,
in order to arrive at what one hates,
how could one not be deluded by power and profit!
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"People know one thing,
but know nothing else."
This is what it means.
17.2 Zǐ Shí 登 Dēng Wú Shān 子石 ascended Mount Wú and looked around,
sighing deeply,
saying:
"Alas,
how sad!
There are those in the world who are clear about the facts of a situation
but do not accord with the desires of the people;
and there are those who accord with the desires of the people
but are not clear about the facts of a situation."
A disciple asked:
"What do you mean?"
Zǐ Shí said:
"In the past, King Fūchāi of Wú did not listen to Wǔ Zǐxū's exhaustive and loyal remonstrations,
gouged out his eyes and executed him.
Tài Zǎi Pǐ and Gōngsūn Luò, seeking only to comply and ingratiate themselves,
followed Fūchāi's desires and attacked Qí,
and the two met their end in the rivers and lakes,
their heads hung from the flags of Yuè.
In the past,
Fèi Zhòng, È Lái, and Jiāo Gé,
with long noses and pierced ears,
Chóng Hóu Hǔ followed the heart of Zhòu,
wishing to accord with his intentions,
but when King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
the four died in the fields of Mù,
their heads and feet in different places.
Bǐ Gān, in his utter loyalty, had his heart cut out and died.
Now, wanting to clarify matters,
I fear the calamity of gouging out eyes and cutting open hearts;
wanting to unite people's hearts,
I fear the misfortune of head and feet being in different places.
Judging from this,
the path of the virtuous is narrow indeed.
Truly, if one does not encounter an enlightened ruler,
within the narrow path,
there will be danger, peril, obstruction, and blockage,
with no way to escape. 」
17.3 Qí Shèzǐ met with King Huì of Qín,
and King Huì was pleased with him.
Thereupon Táng Gū slandered him.
When he met with the king again,
King Huì harbored anger and awaited him.
It was not that his argument was different,
but that the listener had changed.
Thus, taking zhǐ as yǔ [musical notes],
is not the fault of the string;
taking sweet as bitter,
is not the fault of the taste.
17.4 Mí Zixia was favored by the ruler of Wèi.
The law of the state of Wèi stated that
stealing and driving the ruler's carriage was a crime punishable by amputation.
Mí Zixiá's mother fell ill.
Rén wén,
and went at night to tell him that
Mí Zǐxiá had presumptuously driven the ruler's carriage out.
The ruler heard of it and praised him, saying,
"How filial!
For his mother's sake,
he risked the punishment of having his feet cut off!"
He was in an orchard with the ruler,
Mí Zǐxiá ate a peach and found it sweet,
he did not finish it but presented it to the ruler.
The ruler said,
"He loves me so much he forgets his own taste."
When Mí Zǐxiá's beauty faded and the ruler's love waned,
he fell out of favor with the ruler.
The ruler said,
"This is the man who once presumptuously drove my carriage,
and once fed me the remainder of his peach."
Therefore, Zǐxiá's actions
did not necessarily change from the beginning;
that he was first seen as virtuous and later punished
was due to the change in love and hate.
17.5 When Shùn was plowing,
he could not benefit his neighbors,
but when he became the Son of Heaven,
the whole world supported him.
Therefore, a gentleman in poverty cultivates himself,
and in prosperity, he benefits the world.
17.6 Confucius said:
"Since Jìsūn bestowed upon me a thousand zhōng, my friends have become more intimate.
Since Nángōng Jìngshū rode in my carriage, the way has become more practiced.
Therefore, the way is valued after it is timely,
and practiced after there is power.
Without the gift of these two gentlemen,
my way would have nearly been abandoned."
17.7 Tàigōng's fields were not enough to repay the seeds,
his fishing was not enough to repay the nets,
but he had more than enough wisdom to govern the world.
Duke Wén planted rice,
Zēngzǐ raised sheep,
Sūn Shū'áo served as prime minister of Chǔ for three years,
and did not know that the yoke was behind the crossbar.
Those who focus on the big picture naturally forget the small.
Zhì Bó's cook knew about the loss of a skewer of roasted meat,
but Hán and Wèi did not know about their rebellion.
The gardener of Hándān Zǐyáng knew about the loss of a peach,
but he did not know about his own loss.
Those who focus on the small picture also forget the big picture."
17.8 Chúnyú Kūn said to Mencius:
"Those who put reputation before substance
are for others;
those who put reputation after substance
are for themselves.
You were among the three chief ministers,
"To not even consider the relative position of superiors and inferiors before leaving,
is that truly how the benevolent behave?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"To occupy a lower position and not serve the unworthy with their worth is
Bó Yí's way;
to serve Tāng five times and Jié five times is
Yī Yǐn's way;
to not detest a foul ruler and not decline a petty office is
Liǔxià Huì's way.
These three men have different paths,
but their aim is the same.
What is this sameness?
It is:
benevolence.
The gentleman is simply benevolent,
why must they be the same?"
He said:
"During the time of Duke Mù of Lǔ,
Gōngyí Zǐ was in charge of the government,
Zǐ Sī and Zǐ Gēng were ministers,
yet the decline of Lǔ was even more severe.
If that is so,
the worthy are of no benefit to the state."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Yú perished because it did not employ Bǎilǐ Xī,
while Duke Mù of Qín became a hegemon by employing him.
Therefore, not employing the worthy leads to ruin,
how could decline be avoided?"
He said:
"In the past, Wáng Bào lived in Qí,
and west of the Yellow River were skilled at singing ballads;
Mián Qū lived in Gāotáng,
and east of Qí were skilled at singing songs;
Huá Zhōu and the wife of Qǐ Liáng
were skilled at crying for their husbands, thus changing the customs of the state.
What is within
must manifest on the outside.
Those who do the work without achieving the result,
Kūn has never seen.
Therefore, there are no worthy men,
if there were, Kūn would surely recognize them."
He said:
"Kǒngzǐ was the Minister of Justice of Lǔ but was not employed.
When attending a sacrifice,
the distributed sacrificial meat did not arrive,
so he left without removing his ceremonial cap.
Those who did not understand thought it was for the meat,
those who understood thought it was for the lack of propriety.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ wanted to leave on account of a minor offense,
not wanting to leave without a cause.
Therefore, what a gentleman does,
the common people certainly cannot understand."
17.9 When the Chancellor of Liáng died,
Huìzi intended to go to Liáng.
While crossing the river, he suddenly fell into the water.
A boatman rescued him.
The boatman said,
"Where do you want to go that you are in such a hurry?"
He said,
"Liáng Wúxiàng [梁無相] is without a prime minister,
and I want to go and be his prime minister."
The boatman said,
"You are in trouble even here among the boats and oars.
Without me, you would be dead.
How can you be the prime minister of Liáng [梁]?"
Huìzi [惠子] said,
"Living among boats and oars,
then I am not as good as you.
As for pacifying the state and preserving the altars of the soil and grain,
your comparison to me
is like a blind puppy that has never seen."
17.10 Xī Lǘ Guò [西閭過] was crossing the river to the east and drowned in the middle of the river.
He drowned in the middle of the river.
A boatman pulled him out.
The boatman asked him,
"Where did you want to go just now?"
Xī Lǘ Guò [西閭過] said,
"I wanted to go east to persuade the feudal lords and kings."
The boatman covered his mouth and laughed, saying,
"You drowned in the middle of the river while crossing it,
and you cannot even save yourself.
How can you persuade the feudal lords?"
Xī Lǘ said:
"There is nothing for which we can injure each other with your abilities.
Have you not heard of the jade of Hé Shì?
Its value is a thousand gold pieces,
but if you use it to wind thread,
it is not as good as a tile or brick;
The pearl of Suí Hóu,
is a treasure of the state,
but if you use it to shoot magpies,
it is not as good as a mud pellet;
The qíjì and lù'ěr horses,
leaning on the crossbar and bearing the yoke as they gallop,
traveling a thousand *lǐ* in a day,
this is ultimate speed,
but if you use them to catch mice,
they are not as good as a hundred-cash cat;
Gān Jiàng and Mò Yé (swords),
if you strike a bell with them, they do not clang,
if you test them on objects, they are not recognized,
if you raise their blades, they can sever metal,
they can cut feathers and carve iron axes,
this is ultimate sharpness,
but if you use them to repair shoes,
they are not as good as a two-cash awl.
Now, you hold an oar and ride a small boat,
in the middle of a wide expanse of water,
facing the waves of Yáng Hóu and overlooking the deep currents,
this is what you are capable of;
"If you were really to go east and persuade the feudal lords and kings,
upon seeing the ruler of a state,
your muddled state
would be no different from that of a dog that hasn't yet seen anything."
17.11 Gān Wù was sent as an envoy to Qí.
Crossing the great river,
the boatman said:
"The river water
is only between (ankle and knee) deep.
If you cannot cross it yourself,
how can you persuade kings?"
Gān Wù said:
"Not so.
You do not understand.
Things each have their strengths and weaknesses.
Being cautious, sincere, and upright
makes one fit to serve a lord,
but not to command troops.
Qíjì and Lù'ěrdì,
whose hooves can cover a thousand *lǐ*,
if placed in palaces
and made to catch mice,
would be less capable than a small wildcat.
Gān Jiàng was sharp,
his name known throughout the world,
but in using wood,
a craftsman is not as good as an axe.
今持楫而上下隨流， Now, if you hold an oar and go up and down with the current,
吾不如子， I am not as good as you.
說千乘之君、萬乘之主， But if you talk to the rulers of states with a thousand chariots or ten thousand chariots,
子亦不如戊矣 。 」 you are also not as good as Wù."
17．12 今夫世異則事變， Now, if the times change, then affairs change;
事變則時移， if affairs change, then the times shift;
時移則俗易， if the times shift, then customs alter.
是以君子先相其土地而裁其器 ， Therefore, the noble person first assesses the land and then makes the implements,
觀其俗而和其風， observes the customs and harmonizes the manners,
總眾議而定其教。 gathers all opinions and then decides on the teachings.
愚人有學遠射者， There was a foolish man who learned to shoot far;
參天而發， he aimed at the sky and shot,
已射五步之內， and then, having shot within five paces,
又復參天而發。 again he aimed at the sky and shot.
世以易矣， The world has already changed,
不更其儀 ， yet he does not change his methods.
譬如愚人之學遠射。 This is like the foolish man learning to shoot far.
目察秋毫之末者 ， Eyes that observe the tip of an autumn hair
視不能見太山， cannot see Mount Tài.
耳聽清濁之調者， Ears that hear the clear and turbid tones
不聞雷霆之聲， do not hear the sound of thunder.
何也？ Why is this?
唯其意有所移也。 It is only because their focus has shifted.
百人操觿， If a hundred people wield awls,
不可為固結； they cannot make a firm knot.
千人謗獄， If a thousand people slander a just judgment,
不可為直辭； it cannot be called a straightforward verdict.
To be criticized by ten thousand people is
not the way to become a prominent gentleman.
17.13 Deer form herds,
tigers and leopards avoid them;
flying birds form rows,
eagles and vultures do not attack them;
when people gather in crowds,
sages do not offend them.
The *téng* snake wanders in mist and dew,
rides the wind and rain to travel,
and does not stop unless it travels a thousand *lǐ*.
Yet in the evening, it lodges in the holes of loaches and eels.
Why is this so?
Because its focus is not singular.
Now, earthworms have no strong muscles or bones inside,
and no sharp claws or teeth outside,
yet they drink from the Yellow Springs below
and cultivate the dry soil above.
Why is this so?
Because their focus is singular.
The perceptive hear,
the insightful see.
When perception and insight are manifested, benevolence and love become prominent, and integrity and shame are distinguished.
Therefore, if one acts contrary to the proper way,
though one labors, one will not achieve success.
If one seeks what one does not possess,
though one is strong, one will not obtain it.
The wise do not engage in matters outside their purview;
the incorrupt do not seek what is not rightfully theirs.
Therefore, they stay away from harm and their reputation is manifest.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Neither envious nor greedy,
what is there that is not good?"
This is what it means.
17.14 King Zhāo of Chǔ summoned Confucius,
intending to have him take charge of the government and enfeoff him with a territory of seven hundred *shè* (*shè*: a unit of land measurement, usually translated as communities or settlements).
Zǐ Xī said to the King of Chǔ:
"Among your Majesty's ministers, are there any who are as skilled in military matters as Zǐ Lù?
Are there any who can negotiate with the feudal lords as well as Zǎi Yǔ?
Are there any who can manage the five offices of government as well as Zǐ Gòng?
In the past, King Wén resided in Fēng,
and King Wǔ resided in Hào.
Within the area between Fēng and Hào,
a hundred chariots' worth of land,
they attacked their superior and killed their lord,
establishing themselves as the Son of Heaven.
The world all called them sage kings.
Now, with the worthiness of Confucius,
and the land of seven hundred *shè* communities,
and with the assistance of his three disciples,
it would not be to the benefit of Chǔ."
The King of Chǔ then stopped the appointment.
Indeed, the distinction between good and evil is difficult to discern;
even a sage is uniquely subjected to suspicion,
How much more so for the virtuous?
Therefore, sages and worthies rarely unite,
while flattery and sycophancy constantly flourish.
Thus, there are thousands of years of chaos,
but not even a hundred years of good governance.
Kǒngzǐ's 孔子 being doubted,
is it not lamentable!
17.15 Lǔ Āigōng 魯哀公 asked Kǒngzǐ 孔子, saying:
"Do wise men live long?"
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"Yes.
There are three kinds of death that are not due to fate,
but which people bring upon themselves.
Those who rest and rise at improper times,
who are immoderate in eating and drinking,
and who indulge in excessive ease or labor,
are killed by disease.
Those who hold a lower position but offend their lord above,
who have insatiable desires and are relentless in their pursuit,
are killed by punishment.
Those who, being few, offend the many,
who, being weak, insult the strong,
and who, in anger, do not consider their strength,
are killed by weapons.
These three deaths are not due to fate,
but are brought upon oneself."
The *Shī* 詩 (Book of Poetry) says:
"A person without propriety,
what is the point of not dying?"
This is what it means.
17.16 Confucius encountered hardship in the territory between Chen and Cai,
cut off from provisions,
the disciples all showed signs of hunger,
Confucius sang between two pillars.
Zǐlù entered and said:
"Master's singing,
is it proper?"
Confucius did not answer,
when the song ended, he said:
"Yóu,
a gentleman enjoys music,
in order to avoid arrogance;
a petty person enjoys music,
in order to avoid fear.
Who knows this?
You do not understand me, yet you follow me?"
Zǐlù was displeased,
took up a shield and danced,
finished three times and went out.
After seven days,
Confucius continued his music without stopping,
Zǐlù resentfully came to see him,
and said:
"Master's continuing his music,
Shí hū?" (Is it the right time?)
Kǒngzǐ bù yìng, (Confucius did not answer,)
yuè zhōng ér yuē: (when the music ended, he said:)
"Yóu, (Yóu,)
xīzhě Qí Huán bà xīn shēng yú Jǔ, (in the past, the hegemonic ambition of Duke Huán of Qí arose in Jǔ,)
Gōujiàn bà xīn shēng yú Kuàijī, (the hegemonic ambition of Gōujiàn arose in Kuàijī,)
Jìn Wén bà xīn shēng yú Líshì. (the hegemonic ambition of Duke Wén of Jìn arose in Líshì.)
Gù jū bù yōu zé sī bù yuǎn, (Therefore, if one does not live in seclusion, thoughts will not be far-reaching,)
shēn bù yuē zé zhì bù guǎng, (if one's body is not restrained, then wisdom will not be broad,)
yōng zhī ér bù yù zhī." (how could one know, and yet not encounter such things.")
Yúshì xīng. (Then he arose.)
Míngrì, (The next day,)
miǎn yú è, (he was freed from the difficult straits,)
Zǐgòng zhí pèi yuē: (Zǐgòng held the reins and said:)
"Èr, sānzi cóng fūzǐ ér yù cǐ nán yě, (You two or three, following the master and encountering this difficulty,)
qí bùkě wàng yǐ." (should not forget it.)"
Kǒngzǐ yuē: (Confucius said:)
"È! (Bah!)
Shì hé yě? (What is this?)
Yǔ bù yún hū, (Does the saying not go,)
sān zhé gōng ér chéng liángyī. (that a doctor with a thrice-broken arm becomes a good physician.)
Fū Chén Cài zhī jiān, (Being between Chén and Cài,)
Qiū zhī xìng yě. (is fortunate for Qiū.)
Èr, sānzi cóng Qiū zhě, (You two or three who follow Qiū,)
jiē xìng yě. (are all fortunate.)
Wǒ wén zhī, (I have heard that,)
rénjūn bù kùn bù chéng wáng, (a ruler who is not distressed will not become a king,)
lièshì bù kùn bù chéng háng. (and a gentleman who is not distressed will not achieve success.)
昔者 Tāng kùn yú Lǚ,
King Wén was trapped in Yǒulǐ,
Duke Mù of Qín was trapped in Xiáo,
Duke Huán of Qí was trapped in Chángsháo,
Gōujiàn was trapped in Kuàijī,
Duke Wén of Jìn was trapped in Líshì.
As for the Way of being trapped,
it goes from cold to warmth,
and from warmth to cold.
Only the wise understand it and find it difficult to speak of.
The "Book of Changes" says:
"Kùn (Distress),
Hēng (success),
Zhēn (perseverance).
The great man is fortunate,
without blame.
If one speaks, one will not be believed."
What sages find difficult to speak about with people,
is believable."
17.17 Kǒngzǐ was trapped between Chén and Cài,
living in a small, confined space,
seated on a mat used for studying the Three Classics,
not eating for seven days,
with thin quinoa soup without added grain,
the disciples all showed signs of hunger,
but they read the "Book of Poetry" and the "Book of Documents,"
and practiced rituals and music without ceasing.
Zǐ Lù stepped forward to remonstrate, saying:
"Generally, when people do good,
Heaven rewards them with blessings;
when they do not good,
Heaven repays them with misfortune.
Now, Teacher, you have accumulated virtue and done good for a long time,
could it be that you still have some shortcomings in your conduct,
why do you live in seclusion?"
Confucius said:
"Yóu,
you do not understand.
Sit down,
I will tell you.
Do you think that a knowledgeable person knows everything?
Then why did Wángzǐ Bǐgān have his heart cut out and die?
Do you think that those who give advice are always listened to?
Then why did Wǔ Zixū have his eyes gouged out at the east gate of Wú?
Do you think that those who are incorruptible are sure to be employed?
Then why did Bó Yí and Shū Qí starve to death at the foot of Mount Shǒuyáng?
Do you think that those who are loyal are sure to be employed?
Then why did Bào Zhuāng have his flesh wither away,
and Jīng Gōngzǐ Gāo remain obscure throughout his life?
Bào Jiāo embraced a tree and withered standing,
and Jiè Zǐtuī climbed a mountain and was burned to death?
Therefore, there are many gentlemen who are learned and deeply thoughtful but do not meet with the right time,
how can it be only Qiū!
Being virtuous or unworthy
depends on talent;
doing or not doing
depends on man;
meeting with the right time or not
depends on the time;
life and death
depend on fate."
If one possesses talent but does not encounter the right time,
then even with talent, it will not be used.
If one happens to encounter the right time,
what difficulty is there?
Therefore, Shùn tilled Lìshān and made pottery on the banks of the river,
and was established as the Son of Heaven,
which was his encounter with Yáo;
Fù Yuè carried earth in baskets,
abandoned his ramming board and was established as a minister assisting the Son of Heaven,
which was his encounter with Wǔ Dīng;
Yī Yǐn,
was originally a concubine's slave of the Shēnshì family,
carried pots and utensils,
seasoned the five flavors and was established as a prime minister assisting the Son of Heaven,
which was his encounter with Chéng Tāng;
When Lǚ Wàng was fifty years old,
he sold food at Jíjīn,
when he was seventy years old,
he butchered cattle at Cháogē,
when he was ninety years old,
he became a teacher of the Son of Heaven,
which was his encounter with Wén Wáng;
Guǎn Yíwú was bound and gagged,
confined in a prison cart.
From within the cart, he rose to become Zhòngfù (Second Father),
such was his encounter with Qí Huángōng;
Bǎilǐ Xī sold himself for the price of five sheepskins,
and herded sheep for the Bó family,
and he was elevated to the position of high minister,
such was his encounter with Qín Mùgōng;
Shěn Yǐn's name was known throughout the land,
and he was made Lìngyǐn (Prime Minister),
but yielded the position to Sūn Shū'áo,
such was his encounter with Chǔ Zhuāngwáng;
Wǔ Zixū formerly accomplished much,
but was later executed,
it was not that his wisdom had declined,
but that he formerly encountered Hélǘ,
and later encountered Fūchāi.
A fine horse (jì) is burdened by a broken salt cart,
but it is not that it lacks the qualities of a fine horse;
it is that the world is unable to recognize it.
If a fine horse obtained Wáng Liáng and Zàofù (famous charioteers),
would it lack the ability to run a thousand *lǐ*?
Orchids and *zhī* (a type of fungus) grow in the deep forest,
not because they are unwilling to be fragrant without people.
Therefore, learning
is not for the sake of being understood,
but for the sake of not being distressed when in poverty,
and for not allowing one's ambition to decline when worried.
This is the beginning of foreknowing misfortune and fortune, and the mind is not confused.
The sage's deep contemplation is unique in knowledge and unique in vision.
Shùn 舜 was also a wise sage.
He faced south and governed the world,
only because he encountered Yáo 堯.
If Shùn 舜 had lived in the era of Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂,
it would have been commendable for him to have avoided punishment and execution,
what official position could he have obtained to govern?
Now, Jié 桀 killed Guān Lóngféng 關龍逄 and Zhòu 紂 killed Prince Bǐgān 比干.
At that time,
how could Guān Lóngféng 關龍逄 have been ignorant and Bǐgān 比干 have been unwise!
It was simply that Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂 were rulers of a wayward era.
Therefore, the noble person studies diligently,
cultivates oneself and uprightly acts,
in order to await his time."
17.18 Kǒngzǐ 孔子 went to Sòng 宋.
Kuāng Jiǎnzǐ 匡簡子 was about to kill Yáng Hǔ 陽虎.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 resembled him.
Soldiers surrounded Kǒngzǐ's 孔子 residence.
Zǐlù 子路 was angry
and, brandishing his halberd, was about to go down to fight.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 stopped him, saying,
"How can benevolence and righteousness not avoid the customs of the age?
The *Shī* 《詩》 (Book of Odes) and *Shū* 《書》 (Book of Documents) not being studied,
the rites and music not being cultivated,
that is my fault.
As for resembling Yáng Hǔ 陽虎,
Then it is not Qiū's fault,
it is fate!
Yóu, sing,
I will harmonize with you."
Zǐlù sang,
Kǒngzǐ harmonized with him,
and after three rounds, the armored men dispersed.
17.19 Kǒngzǐ said:
"If one does not observe from a high bank,
how can one know the danger of falling;
if one does not look into a deep abyss,
how can one know the danger of drowning;
if one does not observe the sea,
how can one know the danger of wind and waves.
Isn't the loss due to not being aware of these?
A scholar should be cautious of these three things,
and not be a burden to others."
17.20 Zēngzǐ said:
"The echo does not refuse the sound,
the mirror does not refuse the form,
the gentleman rectifies one thing, and all things are accomplished.
Now, walking is not done for the sake of the shadow, yet the shadow follows it;
calling is not done for the sake of the echo, yet the echo responds to it.
Therefore, the gentleman first accomplishes the merit, and then the fame follows."
17.21 Zǐxià asked Zhòngní, saying:
"What kind of person is Yán Yuān?
What about them?"
He said:
"Huí's trustworthiness
is superior to mine, Qiū."
He said:
"What kind of person is Zǐ Gòng?"
What is he like?"
He said:
"Cì's quickness
is superior to mine, Qiū."
He said:
"What kind of person is Zǐ Lù?"
What is he like?"
He said:
"Yóu's courage
is superior to mine, Qiū."
He said:
"What kind of person is Zǐ Zhāng?"
What is he like?"
He said:
"Shī's solemnity
is superior to mine, Qiū."
Thereupon Zǐ Xià left his mat and asked, saying:
"In that case, why do these four serve you, Master?"
He said:
"Sit down,
and I will tell you.
Huí is able to be trustworthy but unable to reflect,
To grant ability that is quick but unyielding,
valor that is brave but without timidity,
a teacher that is dignified but not conforming.
To possess all these four qualities,
Qiū (Confucius) will not do. "
The so-called truly sage person
must see the benefits of advancing and retreating, and the uses of yielding and stretching.
17.22 Dōngguō Zǐ Huì asked Zǐgòng, saying:
"The Master's gate,
how is it so mixed?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Beside the shaping frame are many crooked pieces of wood,
at the gate of a good doctor are many sick people,
beside the grindstone are many dull and blunt things.
The Master cultivates the Way to await the world,
those who come do not stop,
therefore it is mixed."
The *Book of Odes* says:
"Luxuriant are those willows,
cicadas chirping incessantly,
there are deep pools,
reeds and rushes grow abundantly."
Speaking of the side of a great thing,
it accepts everything.
17.23 In the past,
Nánxiá Zǐ visited Chéng Běnzǐ,
Běnzi cooked salamander for him.
Nánxiázi said:
"I have heard that a gentleman does not eat salamander."
Chéng Běnzi said:
"Is it that only gentlemen do not eat it?
What business is it of yours?"
Nánxiázi said:
"I have heard that a gentleman emulates those above him in order to broaden his virtue,
and emulates those below him in order to restrain his conduct.
Emulating the good is
a step towards self-improvement;
emulating the wicked is
the source of self-degradation.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
'High mountains are looked up to,
Broad roads are followed.'
How dare I presume to consider myself a gentleman?
I only aspire to it."
Confucius said:
"When you see a worthy person, think of emulating them;
when you see an unworthy person, examine yourself inwardly."
17.24 Confucius was observing the Lüliáng rapids,
where the water cascaded down forty *rèn*,
circling around for ninety *lǐ*.
Fish and turtles could not pass through,
neither could soft-shelled turtles and alligators dare to dwell there.
There was a man just about to wade into it.
Confucius sent someone to stop him by the cliff, saying:
"This waterfall is forty *rèn* high,
and the circulating current is ninety *lǐ*,
fish and turtles dare not pass,
soft-shelled turtles and crocodiles dare not dwell there,
meaning that it is difficult to cross."
The man did not misunderstand the intention,
and then crossed and came out.
Confucius asked:
"Are you skillful?
Or do you have a special technique?
What is the reason you were able to enter and exit?"
The man replied:
"When I first entered,
I first used loyalty and trustworthiness,
and when I came out,
I again followed with loyalty and trustworthiness.
I placed my body in the current,
and I dared not use selfishness,
that is why I was able to enter and return."
Confucius said to his disciples:
"Even water can be approached with loyalty and trustworthiness for a long time, and you can become close to it,
how much more so with people!"
17.25 Zǐlù, dressed in formal attire, went to see Confucius.
Confucius said:
"Yóu,
what is this swaying appearance?
昔者 Jiāng Shuǐ chū yú Mín Shān, In the past, the Jiāng River originated from Mount Mín;
其始也， in its beginning,
大足以濫觴。 it was large enough only to float a cup.
及其至江之津也， But when it reaches the ferry of the Jiāng,
不方舟， without rafts tied together,
不避風， and without avoiding the wind,
則不可渡也。 then it cannot be crossed.
非唯下流眾川之多乎？ Isn't it simply because of the multitude of streams in the lower reaches?
今若衣服甚盛， Now, if your clothes are excessively splendid,
顏色充盈， and your appearance is overly adorned,
天下誰肯加若者哉？」 who in the world would be willing to add anything to you?"
Zǐlù qū ér chū, Zǐlù hurried out,
改服而入， changed his clothes and came back in,
蓋自如也。 appearing more natural.
Kǒngzǐ yuē: Kǒngzǐ said:
「由記之， "Yóu, remember this,
吾語若。 I will tell you.
賁於言者， Adornment in speech
華也； is mere embellishment;
奮於行者， vehemence in action
伐也。 is boastfulness.
夫色智而有能者， One who appears clever and capable
小人也。 is a petty person.
故君子知之為知之， Therefore, a gentleman knows when he knows,
不知為不知， and acknowledges when he doesn't know;
言之要也； that is the essence of speech.
能之為能之， He is able when he is able,
不能為不能， and admits when he is not able;
The utmost of action.
In speech, the essential is wisdom;
in action, the essential is benevolence.
To be both wise and benevolent,
what more could one desire?
Yóu,
the *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Tāng's descent was not slow,
his sage reverence daily ascended."
This is what it means."
17.26 Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"Does the gentleman also have worries?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"No.
The gentleman cultivates his conduct.
When he has not yet attained it,
he delights in his intention.
Once he has attained it,
he also delights in his knowledge.
Therefore, he has joy throughout his life
and no sorrow for a single day.
The petty person is not like this.
When he has not yet attained something,
he worries that he will not attain it.
Once he has attained it,
he fears losing it.
Therefore, he has sorrow throughout his life
not having a single day of joy."
17.27 Kǒngzǐ saw Róng Qǐqí wearing deerskin clothing,
playing the sè and singing.
Kǒngzǐ asked,
"Sir, what are you happy about?"
He replied,
"My joys are many.
Heaven gave birth to all things,
but humans are the most noble,
and I have already attained being human,
this is the first joy;
among humans, males are considered noble,
and I have already attained being male,
this is the second joy;
in life, some do not see the sun and moon and do not escape being swaddled in infancy,
and I am already ninety-five years old,
this is the third joy.
As for poverty,
it is the constant of the scholar;
death,
is the end of the people.
Abiding in the constant and awaiting the end,
what should I worry about?"
17.28 Zēngzǐ said,
"I have heard the Master's three sayings,
but I have not been able to practice them.
The Master sees one good thing in a person and forgets their hundred faults;
this shows that the Master is easy to deal with.
The Master sees good in others
as if he himself possessed it;
this shows that the Master does not contend.
Upon hearing of goodness, he invariably personally practices it
and then speaks of it;
this shows that the Master is capable of labor.
The Master's capability of labor,
the Master's non-contention,
the Master's ease of dealing with things,
I have studied these three sayings of the Master but have not yet been able to put them into practice."
17.29 Confucius said:
"Huí,
it is as if you have four aspects of the way of a gentleman:
strong in governing yourself,
weak in accepting advice,
apprehensive about awaiting emoluments,
careful in maintaining your conduct."
17.30 Zhòng Ní said:
"Shǐ Qiū has three aspects of the way of a gentleman:
not serving in office yet respecting his superiors,
not offering sacrifices yet respecting the spirits,
being able to bend his uprightness to others."
17.31 Confucius said:
"After Qiū dies,
Shāng is daily increasing,
Cì is daily decreasing.
Shāng likes to be with those who are more virtuous than himself,
Cì likes to talk about those who are not as good as himself."
17.32 Kǒngzǐ was about to leave,
it was raining but he had no umbrella.
A disciple said:
"Zǐxià has an umbrella,
you can use it to travel."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Shāng's character,
is very short on wealth.
I have heard that in associating with people,
promote their strengths,
avoid their weaknesses,
therefore, you can last a long time."
17.33 Zǐlù was about to leave,
bidding farewell to Zhòngní, he said:
"May I ask how to obtain affection in new friendships?
How can one make one's few words practical?
How can one constantly be a good person without transgressing?"
Zhòngní said:
"In making new friends and gaining affection,
be loyal;
in making few words practical,
be trustworthy;
in constantly being a good person without transgressing,
Is this ritual?"
17.34 Zǐ Lù was about to depart,
and bid farewell to Zhòng Ní.
Zhòng Ní said:
"Shall I give you a carriage?
Shall I give you some words?"
Zǐ Lù said:
"Please, give me words."
Zhòng Ní said:
"Without strength, one cannot go far;
without labor, there is no achievement;
without loyalty, there are no relatives;
without trust, there is no return;
without respect, there is no propriety.
Be careful with these five things,
and you can last a long time."
17.35 Zēng Zǐ followed Kǒng Zǐ to Qí.
The Duke Jǐng of Qí employed Zēng Zǐ with the rites for lower ministers.
Zēng Zǐ firmly declined.
As he was about to depart,
Yàn Zǐ saw him off and said:
"I have heard that
a gentleman gifting someone with wealth
is not as good as gifting them with words.
Now, the root of the orchid
takes three years to mature.
If orchids are steeped in deer sauce,
once it is done,
they can be exchanged for a fine horse.
It is not that the orchid is beautiful in itself,
but that which it is steeped in is beautiful.
I hope you will carefully consider that which it is steeped in.
Once you have obtained that which is steeped in,
you should also seek that which it is steeped in.
I have heard it said that,
a gentleman in his dwelling must choose a place,
and in his travels must choose a direction.
In his dwelling, he must choose a place,
in order to seek out scholars;
in his travels, he must choose a direction,
in order to cultivate the Dao.
I have heard that reversing constancy and altering nature is caused by desire;
therefore, one cannot but be careful.」
17.36 Confucius said:
"The nature of ordinary people
is that if there is surplus, they become extravagant;
if there is not enough, they become frugal;
if there is no prohibition, they become licentious;
if there is no limit, they go astray;
if they indulge their desires, they are ruined.
Eating and drinking should have measure,
clothing should have moderation,
dwellings should have limits,
The accumulation of wealth has its limits,
carriages and tools have their bounds;
this is how to prevent the source of chaos."
Therefore, measures and standards must be clear,
and good desires must be heeded.
17.37 Confucius said:
"One who is skillful and likes planning will surely be skilled in his work,
one who is brave and likes unity will surely be victorious,
one who is knowledgeable and likes planning will surely succeed.
The foolish are the opposite."
Occupying a high position and monopolizing favor,
focusing on being jealous of the worthy,
is the nature of the foolish.
Having an arrogant spirit and looking lightly on old grievances.
Therefore, when the position is high, it is certain to be dangerous;
when the responsibility is heavy, it is certain to collapse;
when the favor is monopolized, it is certain to be disgraced.
17.38 Confucius said:
"Children who are whipped and beaten
do not follow their father's teaching;
people who are punished with execution
do not follow their ruler's government."
He is saying that harshness is difficult to implement.
Therefore, the gentleman does not make hasty judgments,
does not use coercion,
because he considers them a source of chaos."
17.39 Confucius said:
"To speak all day without neglecting one's own worries,
to act all day without neglecting one's own troubles,
only the wise possess this.
Therefore, fear is what removes trouble,
respect is what overcomes difficulty.
To practice it one's whole life,
yet be ruined by a single word,
can one not be careful!"
17.40 Confucius said:
"If one uses wealth and status to humble oneself before others,
who would not associate with him?
If one uses wealth and status to respect and love others,
who would not be close to him?
Not going against the multitude in speech,
can be called understanding speech.
If one's words are directed towards the multitude,
can be called understanding the times."
17.41 Confucius said:
"As for being wealthy and being able to enrich others,
one may desire poverty, but it cannot be attained;
as for being noble and being able to ennoble others,
one may desire lowliness, but it cannot be attained;
as for being successful and being able to make others successful,
one may desire destitution, but it cannot be attained."
17.42 Zhòng Ní said:
"If you plant something in a place not suited for it,
it will not grow.
If you speak to someone who is not the right person,
they will not listen.
Getting the right person
is like gathering sand and raining on it;
not getting the right person is like gathering deaf people and drumming for them."
17.43 Kǒngzǐ said:
"A boat cannot travel without water,
but if water enters the boat, it will sink.
A ruler cannot govern without the people,
but if the people defy their superiors, the state will collapse."
Therefore, it is said:
"A gentleman must be dignified,
and the common people must be kept in check."
17.44 Kǒngzǐ said:
"Relying on the wise ensures one will not be distressed;
relying on the wealthy ensures one will not be impoverished.
Why does a severed earthworm continue to move?
Because it has many supporting legs."
17.45 Kǒngzǐ said:
"If you do not know a son,
observe his friends;
if you do not know a ruler,
observe his envoys."
It is also said:
"Dwelling with good people
is like entering a room of orchids and *zhǐ* (angelica),
after a long time you don't smell its fragrance,
you have become assimilated to it;
dwelling with bad people
is like entering a stall of salted fish,
after a long time you don't smell its stench,
you have also become assimilated to it."
Therefore, it is said:
"That in which vermilion is stored becomes red,
that in which lacquer is stored becomes black,
the *jūnzǐ* (gentleman) should be careful of that in which he stores things."
17.46 Zǐ Gòng asked, saying:
"When the *jūnzǐ* sees great water, he invariably observes it,
why is that?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"That water is something to which the *jūnzǐ* compares virtue.
Imparting widely and without selfishness,
it is like virtue;
that which it reaches lives,
it is like benevolence;
its flow is low and crooked,
but all follows its principle,
it is like righteousness;
the shallow flows readily,
the deep is unfathomable,
似智; [Resembles wisdom;]
其赴百仞之谷不疑, [Its plunging into a hundred-ren valley without hesitation,]
似勇; [resembles courage;]
綽弱而微達, [Being gentle and weak yet subtly penetrating,]
似察; [resembles discernment;]
受惡不讓, [Receiving filth without rejecting,]
似包蒙; [resembles embracing ignorance;]
不清以入, [Entering unclean,]
鮮潔以出, [emerging fresh and clean,]
似善化; [resembles good transformation;]
主量必平, [Governing with a measure that is certainly level,]
似正; [resembles uprightness;]
盈不求概, [When full, not seeking to level,]
似度; [resembles moderation;]
其萬折必東, [Its ten thousand turns inevitably lead east,]
似意. [resembles intention.]
是以君子見大水觀焉爾也。」 [Therefore, the junzi, seeing great water, contemplates it." ]
17．47 夫智者何以樂水也？ [Why do the wise find pleasure in water?]
曰: [He says:]
泉源潰潰, [The spring's source gushing forth,]
不釋晝夜, [not ceasing day or night,]
其似力者; [resembles strength;]
循理而行, [Following principles in its course,]
不遺小間, [not neglecting the smallest space,]
其似持平者; [resembles maintaining impartiality;]
動而之下, [Moving downwards,]
其似有禮者; [resembles having propriety;]
To go to a ravine thousands of *rèn* deep without hesitation,
it is like having courage;
to remove obstacles and flow clearly,
it is like understanding destiny;
to enter unclearly,
and emerge purely,
it is like being good at transforming;
the multitude takes to leveling,
categories are made right,
the myriad things obtain it and live,
lose it and die,
it is like having virtue;
gentle, gentle, deep, deep,
unfathomable,
it is like being a sage.
Permeating and moistening between heaven and earth,
countries are thereby formed,
this is why the wise find joy in water.
The *Shī* says:
"We think and are happy at the Pàn River,
gathering the *máo* grass,
the Marquis of Lǔ arrives and stops,
drinking wine on the Pàn."
This speaks of finding joy in water.
Now, why do the benevolent find joy in mountains?
It is said:
Mountains are lofty and majestic,
what the myriad people look up to.
Grass and trees grow there,
all things take root there,
flying birds gather there,
running animals rest there,
treasures are cultivated there,
extraordinary people reside there,
nurturing all things without tiring,
taking from all directions without limit.
Clouds and winds emerge,
connecting the vital energy between heaven and earth,
nations are thereby established;
this is why the benevolent find joy in mountains.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Great Mount Tài is majestic,
The Marquis of Lǔ gazes up to it."
This speaks of the joy of mountains.
17.48 Jade has six virtues;
the gentleman values it.
Viewed, it is warm and lustrous;
approached, it is finely textured;
its sound is near, gentle, and heard far away;
it bends but does not break;
when chipped, it does not crumble;
it is sharp but does not cut;
if it has a flaw, it must show it on the outside;
therefore, it is valued.
The quality of being warm and lustrous in appearance,
The gentleman compares himself to virtue in it;
those who are close to the dense grains,
the gentleman compares himself to wisdom in them;
those whose sound is gentle up close yet heard from afar,
the gentleman compares himself to righteousness in them;
those who bend but do not yield,
those who are chipped but not weakened,
the gentleman compares himself to courage in them;
those who are upright but not harsh,
the gentleman compares himself to benevolence in them;
those whose flaws must be seen on the outside,
the gentleman compares himself to emotions in them.
17.49 Dào Wú heard from Master [Confucius],
having much knowledge, having no knowledge,
which of these is better?
The response was:
"The one with no knowledge,
belongs to the category of the dead,
even if not dead,
those burdened by him will surely be numerous.
However, the one with much knowledge,
values his effort,
the one with much knowledge,
if it comes from benefiting others, then it is good,
if it comes from harming others, then it is not good."
Dào Wú said:
"Excellent!"
17.50 Yuè Shífù said: "
The unworthy person considers himself wise,
the foolish person considers himself knowledgeable,
those who are glib and flattering cannot fathom each other's hearts.
They speak whatever comes to mind
and yet tell others not to speak.
It is like digging a well when one is thirsty
or forging weapons only when facing disaster;
though one hastens to act, it is already too late."
17.51 "To forget poverty when facing wealth
and to forget death when facing life
can keep one far from guilt.
The *jūnzǐ* cherishes his words,
the peacock cherishes its feathers,
the tiger and leopard cherish their claws—
these are all principles for cultivating oneself.
Those who associate with superiors will not lose their emolument,
those who associate with inferiors will not escape trouble;
therefore, the *jūnzǐ* chooses those with whom he associates,
just as the farmer chooses the field in which he plants.
The *jūnzǐ* cultivates people,
the farmer cultivates fields.
The farmer chooses the seed to sow;
in a bountiful year, he will surely obtain grain.
The scholar chooses the people to cultivate;
in prosperous times, he will surely obtain emolument."
17.52 Only after the Way is lost in the world do benevolence and righteousness arise;
only after the state is not well governed do filial sons arise;
only after the people contend and do not share fairly do kindness and compassion arise;
only after the Way goes against the times and is reversed do schemes and strategies arise.
17.53 In all cases, the creation of goodness
all come from what is learned.
Within a room,
there must be a guiding principle,
which refers to the parents.
Therefore, if the ruler is upright, the people are well-governed;
if the parents are upright, the children and grandchildren are filial and kind.
Therefore, the children in Kǒngzǐ's 孔子 family do not know how to curse,
the children in Zēngzǐ's 曾子 family do not know (how to stray from the) road.
The reason for this is
that they are born and well-taught.
17.54 The benevolent person likes to unite people,
the unbenevolent person likes to separate people.
Therefore, when a gentleman lives among people, there is order;
when a petty person lives among people, there is chaos.
The gentleman desires to harmonize people,
it's like water and fire which cannot coexist,
but a cauldron is in between,
the water and fire do not become chaotic,
and instead harmonize a hundred flavors.
Therefore, a gentleman must carefully choose the people around him.
17.55 Qí Jǐnggōng 齊景公 asked Ànzǐ 晏子, saying:
"I myself am sitting on the ground,
my ministers are all sitting on the ground,
yet you alone pluck grass to sit on.
Why is that?"
Ànzǐ 晏子 replied:
"Yīng 嬰 has heard that
only during funerals and in prison does one sit on the ground.
Now, I dare not bring the affairs of funerals and prisons
to attend upon the ruler."
17.56 Qí Gāotíng 齊高廷 asked Kǒngzǐ 孔子, saying:
"I do not abandon the mountains,
nor do I take a direct path across the land.
I wear a raincoat,
and carry tools.
With focused energy, I inquire about the way of serving a ruler.
I wish that you, Master, would tell me."
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"Be upright in managing affairs,
be respectful in assisting,
and be tireless in your dealings with people.
When you see a person of virtue, promote them.
When you see a petty person, distance yourself from them.
Discard your evil intentions,
and be loyal to them.
Be quick in your actions,
cultivate your propriety.
Though a thousand *lǐ* away,
they are as close as brothers;
if conduct is not quick-witted,
and rites are not in accord,
those across the gate will not communicate."
Discriminating objects
18.1 Yán Yuān asked Zhòngní, saying:
"What is the conduct of a complete person like?"
The Master said:
"The conduct of a complete person
understands the principles of feelings and nature,
is conversant with the changes of all kinds of things,
knows the reasons for darkness and light,
sees the source of wandering *qì*.
One who is like this can be called a complete person.

"Why is there no hunting in summer?"

Yuē:

The five grains

píng, (everything was) fair,

Yì managed the forests,

Qì managed the Ministry of Education,

The twelve regional governors carried out their duties, and in the nine provinces none dared to deviate from the right path.
Yǔ embanked the nine mountains,
dredged the nine marshes,
opened up the nine roads,
and stabilized the nine provinces.
Each province, according to its duty, came to offer tribute,
not failing in what was appropriate.
It extended five thousand *lǐ*,
even reaching the remote frontier regions.
In the south he pacified Jiāozhǐ, Dàfā, the Western Róng, Xīzhī, Qúsōu, Dī, and Qiāng;
in the north he reached the Shān Róng, Fā, and Sùshèn;
in the east he reached the Cháng Yí and Dǎo Yí.
Within the four seas,
all enjoyed the achievements of Emperor Shùn.
Thereupon, Yǔ created the music of the "Nine Shao,"
and presented exotic objects,
and phoenixes came soaring.
The clear virtue of the world all began with Emperor Yú.
19．20 One who shoots must have a calm mind and upright posture,
Holding a bow and arrows,
examining them carefully to ensure they are sturdy,
only then can the archer be able to hit the target.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"The great target is set up,
bow and arrows are drawn,
the archers are assembled,
show your skill."
This is what it means.
The word *hú* (弧, bow) means *yù* (豫, preparation).
*Yù* (preparation) is
preparing my intention.
Therefore, in ancient times, when a child was born on the third day,
they would use a mulberry bow and artemisia arrows, six of them,
to shoot at heaven and earth in the four directions.
Heaven and earth in the four directions
are what a man is responsible for.
He must have the intention to take on these responsibilities,
then he dares to eat grain.
Therefore, it is said:
"Do not eat for nothing,"
this is what it means.
19.21 Being born and having relationships with others
is why it's called "entertaining guests."
From the Son of Heaven to the scholar, each has his order.
Presenting gifts to the dead that do not reach the coffin,
offering condolences to the living that do not extend to mourning,
This is not in accordance with ritual.
Therefore, in ancient times, a congratulatory journey was fifty *lǐ*,
and a journey to attend a funeral was one hundred *lǐ*.
Gifts of *zèng* and *fèng* and the timing of events are called "time."
Time
is a major element of ritual.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* says:
"The Heavenly King sent Zǎi Xuān to return the *fèng* for Huì Gōng and Zhòng Zǐ."
What is *fèng*?
In funeral affairs, there is the giving of *fèng*,
which is generally in the form of chariot horses and bundles of silk.
Chariots and horses are called *fèng*,
goods and wealth are called *fù*,
clothing and quilts are called *suì*,
food for the mouth is called *hán*,
and treasured items are called *zèng*.
Things given to the living are *fù* and *fèng*,
things given to the dead are *zèng* and *suì*.
*Zèng* and *suì* are for sending off the dead,
*fù* and *fèng* are for assisting the living.
How many chariots and horses, bundles of silk, goods and wealth, clothing and quilts, and treasured items
are given?
It is said:
The Son of Heaven receives six chariot horses,
a feudal lord receives four,
a *dàfū* receives three,
a *yuánshì* receives two,
and a *xiàshì* receives one.
The Son of Heaven (Emperor) has five bundles of silk,
three of black and two of crimson,
each fifty chi (feet) long;
the feudal lords have three of black and two of crimson,
each thirty chi long;
the grand masters have one of black and two of crimson,
each thirty chi long;
the senior officers have one of black and one of crimson,
each two zhang (20 chi) long;
the junior officers have one bolt of patterned silk and one of plain silk each;
the common people have one bolt of cloth and one of silk each.
For the burial gifts (fèng) for the Son of Heaven,
six horses for riding,
and a riding chariot;
the feudal lords have four horses,
and a covered carriage;
the grand masters have a three-horse carriage;
the senior and junior officers do not use carriages.
The Son of Heaven has one set of embroidered clothing,
reaching the ground;
the feudal lords' clothing covers the instep,
the grand masters' clothing reaches the ankles,
and the officers' clothing reaches the thigh.
The Son of Heaven has a pearl placed in the mouth of the deceased,
the feudal lords have jade,
the grand masters have jī-stones (a type of bead),
the officers have shells,
and the common people have grain.
Those whose position is high and whose virtue is profound, and those who are close relatives,
receive generous *fù* (gifts of money), *pèng* (gifts for the burial), *hán* (items placed in the mouth of the deceased), and *suì* (clothing placed on the deceased).
The amounts also vary according to wealth and poverty,
in numbers of two, three, four, and five.
These numbers are derived from Heaven and Earth to establish odd and even numbers.
They are measured according to human feelings to establish appropriate regulations.
This is called "having a reason."
It is a major principle of ritual.
19.22 The *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) says:
"On *gēngxū*,
the Heavenly King died."
The *Zhuàn* (Commentary) says:
"Why is the Heavenly King's burial not recorded?
The Son of Heaven's death is recorded, but not the burial,
because it must be at the proper time.
The death and burial of the feudal lords are recorded,
because when the Son of Heaven is present,
they cannot necessarily choose their own time."
"What does 'must be at the proper time' mean?"
"The Son of Heaven is coffined after seven days and buried after seven months.
The feudal lords are coffined after five days and buried after five months.
The grand officers are coffined after three days and buried after three months.
The *shì* (lower officials) and commoners are coffined after two days and buried after two months.
"Why is it all like this?"
He said:
"The rites do not anticipate misfortune.
Only after death are mourning clothes prepared.
Clothes are made of mourning cloth,
coffins are decorated and repaired,
holes are dug for graves and burial sites,
and then the funeral rites are completed,
all relatives from outside come,
the burial mound is gathered together,
and the kindness and generosity of filial sons and loyal ministers are fully expressed.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven is buried after seven months,
and all who share the same standards arrive;
the feudal lords are buried after five months,
and all who attend the same alliances arrive;
the high officials are buried after three months,
and all who attend the same court arrive;
scholars and commoners are buried after two months,
and all relatives by marriage arrive."
19.23 Yánlíng Jìzǐ went to Qí.
On his return,
his eldest son died between Yíng and Bó,
so he buried him there.
Kǒngzǐ heard of it and said:
"Yánlíng Jìzǐ is
someone from Wú who is familiar with the rites."
He sent Zǐgòng to go and observe it.
The digging of the grave should not reach the springs,
and the wrapping of the body should be done with seasonal clothes.
After the burial, a mound is made,
the grave pit is covered up,
and its height should be such that it can be hidden.
After the mound is made,
one bares the left shoulder,
circles the mound to the right,
and cries out three times,
saying:
"Flesh and bones return to the earth,
it is fate;
but the spirit and breath go everywhere,
go everywhere!"
And then they depart.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yánlíng Jìzǐ in ritual, it is appropriate."
19.24 A child is free from his parents' embrace after three years,
therefore the mourning period is set at three years,
in order to repay the kindness of one's parents.
A one-year mourning period
applies generally to the feudal lords,
and a three-year mourning period
applies generally to the Son of Heaven,
this is the norm of ritual.
19.25 Zǐxià completed the three-year mourning period and
presented himself to Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ gave him a qín (a stringed instrument) and
asked him to tune it.
He picked up the qín and tuned it,
playing it cheerfully and happily.
He rose and said:
"The former kings established ritual,
and I dare not fall short of it."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He is a junzi (gentleman)!"
Mǐn Zǐqiān completed the three-year mourning period and
presented himself to Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ gave him a qín and
asked him to tune it.
He picked up the qín and tuned it,
playing it with sorrow and grief.
He rose and said:
"The former kings established ritual,
and I dare not exceed it."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He is a junzi!"
Zǐgòng asked,
"Mǐn Zǐ's grief was not yet exhausted,

I am confused.
敢問何謂？ 」 May I venture to ask what is meant by that?"

夫三年之喪， Now, the three-year mourning period

劣者之所勉。 」 and the inferior person feels compelled to do."

To extend it to relatives.
Serving the ruler in every matter

19.27 In ancient times, those who suffered disasters were called *lì*.
The ruler would temporarily wear plain clothes,
and dispatch officials to offer condolences to the dead and inquire about the sick,
showing concern with shamans and doctors,
prostrating themselves to rescue them,
and using medicinal porridge to treat them.
Kindness should be prioritized for widows, widowers, orphans, and the solitary.
If they are sick and unable to support themselves,
or if they die and have no means to be buried,
then they should be buried.
Do not call at the gate of those who have a parent's funeral;
those who are observing the mourning periods of *zī shuāi* or *dà gōng*
are exempt from labor service and levies for five months;
those who are observing the mourning period of *xiǎo gōng*,
before the burial,
are exempt from labor service and levies;
in cases where there are multiple corpses and many deaths that are urgent,
then gather many young children,
beat drums and light torches,
entering the official palaces and neighborhoods to use them.
Each beats drums and lights torches,
driving away (evil influences) from the official palaces and neighborhoods.
The head of the household,
Capping
takes place at the eastern steps.
When the ceremony is finished,
one goes out by the village gate,
one goes out by the city gate,
and proceeds to the open country.
This is the way to crawl and escape from misfortune.
It is the same when the army suffers a great defeat.
19.28 In fasting,
one thinks of where they resided,
one thinks of their smiles and words,
one thinks of what they did.
After fasting for three days,
one can then see the person for whom the fast is undertaken.
On the day of the sacrifice,
about to enter the door,
one dimly seems to see their appearance,
circling and leaving the door,
one sighs as if one hears the sound of their sighs.
The appearance of the ancestors is constantly before one's eyes;
their voices and coughs,
constantly ring in one's ears;
their likes and dislikes,
are not forgotten in one's heart.
This is the fast of a filial son.
19.29 The spring sacrifice is called *cí*,
The summer sacrifice is called Yuè (禴),
the autumn sacrifice is called Cháng (嘗),
the winter sacrifice is called Zhēng (烝).
In spring, leeks and eggs are offered,
in summer, wheat and fish are offered,
in autumn, millet and pork are offered,
in winter, rice and geese are offered.
A Xiá (祫) is held once every three years,
a Dì (禘) is held once every five years.
Xiá (祫) means
"to unite";
Dì (禘) means
"to examine."
Xiá (祫) is a
grand united sacrifice at the ancestral temple;
Dì (禘) is
to examine their virtue and differentiate the superior from the inferior.
When a sage ruler is about to sacrifice,
he must purify himself with fasting and concentrate his thoughts,
as if his ancestors were present.
Before beginning and while still preparing,
being respectful and attentive,
focusing solely on imagining the countenance of his ancestors faintly appearing,
this is the sincerity of a filial son.
Those from the four directions who assist in the sacrifice,
come empty and return full,
arrive vacant and go back laden,
all taking their models from it.
19.30 Hán Hèzi was crossing the river.
The ferryman told him,
"Of the people who pass by here,
there has never been one who did not enjoy a comfortable ride.
Why don't you enjoy one?"
Hán Hèzi said,
"The Son of Heaven sacrifices to the gods within the seas,
the feudal lords sacrifice within their borders,
the grand officers sacrifice to their relatives,
and the scholars sacrifice to their ancestors.
I, Hè, have not yet had the opportunity to serve the River God."
The ferryman pushed his oar harder,
and the boat shipped water and drifted.
The ferryman said,
"Just now the servant had already warned you.
You did not listen to the servant's words.
Now the boat is shipping water and drifting,
which is very dangerous.
Why not adjust your clothing and swim ashore?"
Hánzi said,
"I will not change my will because people dislike me,
nor will I change my principles because I am about to die."
Before he had finished speaking,
the boat drifted away rapidly.
Hán Hèzi said,
"The *Shī* says,
'Thickly grows the kudzu vine,
Shī yú tiáo méi,
the gentle and kind gentleman,
seeks blessings without turning back."
Even ghosts and spirits do not turn back,
how much less so would people?
19.31 Confucius said:
"Rituals without form,
are reverence;
mourning without garments,
is sorrow;
music without sound,
is joy.
To be trusted without speaking,
to be awe-inspiring without moving,
to be benevolent without giving,
is will (or purpose).
The sound of bells and drums,
if struck in anger, is martial;
if struck in sorrow, is sad;
if struck in joy, is happy.
When the will changes,
the sound also changes.
If the will is sincere,
it penetrates metal and stone,
how much more so does it affect people?"
19.32 Gōng Mèngzǐ Gāo saw Zhuānsūn Zǐ Mò and said:
「Gǎn wèn jūnzǐ zhī lǐ hérú? 」[How may I venture to ask, what is the proper conduct of a *jūnzǐ*?]
Zhuānsūn Zǐ Mò yuē: [Zhuānsūn Zǐ Mò said:]
「Qù ěr wài lì, [Rid yourself of outward harshness,]
yǔ ěr nèi , [and with your inner [self]],
sè shèng ér xīn zì qǔ zhī, [if appearance prevails and the mind takes things on its own,]

Gōng Mèng bùzhī, [Gōng Mèng did not understand,]
yǐ gào Zēngzǐ, [and told Zēngzǐ about it.]
Zēngzǐ qiǎo rán qūnxún yuē: [Zēngzǐ, looking grave and hesitant, said:]

19．33 Zēngzǐ yǒu jí, [Zēngzǐ was ill,]
Mèng Yí wǎng wèn zhī. [Mèng Yí went to inquire about him.]
Zēngzǐ yuē: [Zēngzǐ said:]

wú yǔ rǔ. [I will tell you.]

As for placing the wine vessels and stands,
arranging the bamboo dishes and wooden bowls,
these are the duties of the officers;
even if a gentleman is not able to do them,
